traveler: Los Catorce Santos Ayudantes (the Fourteen Holy Helpers, Vierzehn Nothelfer)
title: The Company of Fourteen: from the Martyrs' Graves to the Meadow at Langheim
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Montmartre, the bishop beheaded on the hill
stops.date_confidence: traditional; en.wikipedia gives c. 250 for the martyrdom and treats the cephalophore legend as legend
stops.campa: Denis, sent from Rome to be the first bishop of Lutetia, is taken with his priest and his deacon and beheaded on the hill above the city that the Romans call the mount of Mercury and the Christians will call the mount of martyrs. He rises with his head in his hands and walks north, preaching, until the ground he has chosen stops him, and there a woman buries him. Twelve hundred years later a shepherd in Franconia will count him among fourteen children standing in a field, and the count will hold.
stops.quote: O GOD, who didst confer Thy saving faith on the people of France through Thy holy bishop and martyr Dionysius, and didst glorify him before and after his martyrdom by many miracles.
stops.quote_source: Bonaventure Hammer, Mary, Help of Christians, and the Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part IV, Novena in Honor of St. Dionysius
suggested_refs: The hill of Montmartre and the martyrium tradition of the first bishop of Paris
sources: Hammer, Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part IV

stops.name: Via Salaria, the deacon buried by the road
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Cyriacus, deacon of Rome, is tortured and beheaded under Diocletian and laid in the ground along the Via Salaria with the companions who die beside him. The legend that grows around the grave has him carrying water to the enslaved labourers raising the Baths of Diocletian, into the cutting where men die of the work; the persecution that kills him is paid for, in part, by their stone. He becomes the helper invoked against possession, and against temptation at the hour of death.
suggested_refs: The catacomb burials of the Via Salaria; the later translations to Santa Maria in Via Lata and to Altorf in Alsace

stops.name: Byzantium, the centurion under two names
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the member of the Fourteen is standardly identified as Agathius of Byzantium, but the dedicatee of the early Constantinopolitan church of Saint Acacius is not settled
stops.campa: Agathius, a Cappadocian serving as centurion in the Roman garrison, is scourged and beheaded at Byzantium before Constantine gives the city his name. A church of Saint Acacius stands here early enough that nobody records its founding, and more than one martyr of that name could own it. The company of fourteen takes him under the name Acacius and gives him the headache and the fear of dying without warning. It does not trouble to say which Acacius he is, and no later council settles the question on its behalf.
suggested_refs: The early church of Saint Acacius at Constantinople, dedicatee disputed

stops.name: Lydda, the soldier's tomb at Diospolis
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia treats Lydda as the place of martyrdom and burial and calls the Nicomedia setting secondary
stops.campa: George, a soldier of the eastern army, refuses the sacrifice and is killed at Diospolis in Palestine, which the Arabs will call Lod. He is buried in the town of his mother's people, and under Constantine a titular church rises over the grave; the crypt still shows a sarcophagus, described by those who describe it carefully as a symbolic tomb. From here his name travels further than any of the other thirteen, into Georgia, England, Ethiopia, Catalonia. In the German company he is asked for the health of cattle.
stops.quote: Domestic animals, too, being attacked by the plague, Sts. George, Erasmus, Pantaleon, and Vitus were invoked for their protection.
stops.quote_source: Bonaventure Hammer, Mary, Help of Christians, and the Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part III, Chapter I
suggested_refs: The Church of Saint George at Lod and its crypt sarcophagus
sources: Hammer, Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part III

stops.name: Nicomedia, the physician denounced by physicians
stops.date_confidence: attested; birth c. 275, martyrdom c. 305
stops.campa: Pantaleon, physician to the emperor Maximian, is denounced by rival doctors and executed at Nicomedia in the last and worst of the persecutions. The legend holds that his blood, gathered at the killing, liquefies once a year at Ravello on the Amalfi coast, a thousand kilometres from the block where it was spilled. He treats the poor without a fee while he lives, and after death he is asked for the same service, becoming the helper of physicians, of midwives, and of livestock dying in the byre.
suggested_refs: The annual liquefaction of the blood of Pantaleon at Ravello

stops.name: Sebastea, the bishop and the wool-combs
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Blaise, bishop of Sebastea in Lesser Armenia, is arrested during the persecution of Licinius, torn with iron wool-combs, and beheaded by order of the governor Agricola. On the road to the prison a mother brings him a child choking on a fishbone, and the bone comes free. He asks, before he dies, that whoever calls on him for the throat, or for any other sickness, be heard. Of the whole company he is the one whose blessing is still given by name, two candles crossed at the neck each third of February.
stops.quote: And S. Blase prayed to our Lord tofore his death that whosoever desired his help from the infirmity of the throat, or required aid for any other sickness or infirmity, that he would hear him, and might deserve to be guerished and healed.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, trans. William Caxton (1483), Life of St Blaise; Fordham Medieval Sourcebook
suggested_refs: The blessing of throats with crossed candles on 3 February
sources: Caxton, The Golden Legend (1483), Life of St Blaise

stops.name: Chalcedon, the martyrium for Christopher
stops.date_confidence: attested; built 450-452
stops.campa: Within two centuries of the death ascribed to him, a martyrium to Christopher goes up at Chalcedon across the water from Constantinople, the earliest fixed address of a cult with no reliable biography behind it. The Greeks make him a giant with the head of a dog, taken from the tribes at the edge of the map; the Latins make him a ferryman who carries a child across a river and finds the child heavier than the world. Both versions reach Franconia. The shepherd will meet the second one.
stops.quote: GREAT St. Christophorus, seeking the strongest and mightiest master thou didst find him in Jesus Christ, the almighty God of heaven and earth, and didst faithfully serve Him with all thy power to the end of thy life, gaining for Him countless souls and finally shedding thy blood for Him; obtain for me the grace to bear Christ always in my heart, as thou didst once bear Him on thy shoulder.
stops.quote_source: Bonaventure Hammer, Mary, Help of Christians, and the Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part IV, Invocation of St. Christophorus
suggested_refs: The Chalcedon martyrium of 450-452, earliest fixed site of the Christopher cult
sources: Hammer, Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part IV

stops.name: Rome, the church of Sant'Eustachio
stops.date_confidence: attested for the church, 731-741; the martyrdom under Hadrian is legend and en.wikipedia calls Eustace a fictitious saint
stops.campa: A church of Sant'Eustachio stands in Rome by the pontificate of Gregory the Second, and this is the first hard evidence of the cult. Everything earlier is story: the Roman general Placidus hunting a stag, the crucifix standing between its antlers, the conversion, the new name, the loss of wife and sons and rank, the roasting alive in a bronze bull. No document places him before the seventh century. The company admits him anyway and gives him to those in family trouble and sudden reversal of fortune.
stops.quote: O GOD, who didst lead Thy holy martyr Eustachius safely through many trials and dangers to the glorious crown of martyrdom.
stops.quote_source: Bonaventure Hammer, Mary, Help of Christians, and the Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part IV, Novena in Honor of St. Eustachius
suggested_refs: Sant'Eustachio in Campo Marzio, attested under Gregory II
sources: Hammer, Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part IV

stops.name: Saint-Denis, the abbot's translation of Vitus
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Abbot Fulrad brings relics of Vitus from Italy to the abbey of Saint-Denis, three centuries before Franconia has heard of a company of fourteen, the culmination of a translation that carries the martyr's bones over the Alps and across half of Francia. The house is already Denis's own burial church and the necropolis of the Frankish kings, so two of the future helpers lie under one roof, and nobody counts them yet. This is Vitus's first Frankish address, carried alone, seven centuries before Regensburg gathers him into any company at all.
stops.quote: ST. VITUS, glorious martyr of Christ; in thy youth thou wast exposed to violent and dangerous temptations, but in the fear of God and for the love of Jesus thou didst victoriously overcome them.
stops.quote_source: Bonaventure Hammer, Mary, Help of Christians, and the Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part IV, Invocation of St. Vitus
suggested_refs: The abbey of Saint-Denis under Abbot Fulrad, holding relics of both Denis and Vitus

stops.name: Corvey, the bones go into Westphalia
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Saint-Denis gives the bones of Vitus on to the new imperial abbey of Corvey on the Weser, and from Corvey the cult moves out through Westphalia and Saxony and eventually into Bohemia. This is the first of the fourteen planted deliberately in German ground by an act of policy rather than by trade or accident. The Saxons, converted by force two generations earlier, take a martyr of Lucania for their own. Thirteen more eastern and Roman dead will come north on the same roads.
suggested_refs: Corvey Abbey on the Weser, receiving Vitus from Saint-Denis in 836

stops.name: Gaeta, Erasmus carried from the burning see
stops.date_confidence: attested for the destruction of Formia in 842; the arrival at Gaeta is dated only as after it
stops.campa: Saracen raiders raze Formia, where Erasmus had been bishop and where the cathedral has kept him since his death, and the townspeople carry what they can up the coast to Gaeta. The relics go with them. Erasmus travels under a second name, Elmo, and takes the sailors with him: the blue fire that plays on a masthead in a storm is called his light. Inland Germany, which has no sea, will keep him instead for pains of the belly, and put a windlass in his hands.
suggested_refs: The transfer of the cult of Erasmus from Formia to Gaeta after the Saracen raid of 842

stops.name: Dubrovnik, the canon's vision and the throat bone
stops.date_confidence: attested as tradition of the city, dated 971 by en.wikipedia
stops.campa: A canon of Ragusa named Stojko sees Blaise in the night and is told that a Venetian fleet lying offshore under pretence of taking on water means to seize the city. The warning goes to the senate, the city arms, the fleet leaves. Ragusa takes the bishop of Sebastea for its patron and builds him a church on the Stradun, and keeps his skull, his throat bone and both his hands in wrought reliquaries. Every third of February they are carried through the streets, and the town is called by his name as often as its own.
suggested_refs: The Church of St Blaise on the Stradun, Dubrovnik, and the 3 February procession of the reliquaries

stops.name: Cologne, the monastery church of Saint Pantaleon
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the church replacing a Roman villa is dated around 870 without a named dedication, and the Pantaleon dedication belongs to the monastery church begun 966 and consecrated 980
stops.campa: On the Rhine, over the ruins of a Roman villa, a monastery church is raised and consecrated to Pantaleon, dead in Nicomedia six and a half centuries before and buried nowhere near. Archbishop Bruno is laid in it; the empress Theophanu, Byzantine wife of Otto the Second, chooses it for her grave. English scholarship will call the Rhineland the birthplace of the fourteen and German scholarship will name Regensburg instead. Whoever is right, the Rhine has a helper's church three hundred years before the count begins.
suggested_refs: St Pantaleon, Cologne, one of the twelve Romanesque churches, burial place of Theophanu

stops.name: Saint-Denis, Suger's altar of Eustace
stops.date_confidence: inferred; en.wikipedia dates the record to Abbot Suger, twelfth century, without a year
stops.campa: Abbot Suger, rebuilding the choir at Saint-Denis into the first Gothic church in France, records at one of its altars the first relics of Eustace to reach Europe. The abbey now holds Denis in the crypt, Eustace on Suger's list, and the memory of Vitus, given away to Corvey four hundred years earlier. Nobody in the Ile-de-France assembles them into a company. The counting will be done elsewhere, in Bavarian dioceses that have none of these bones, by people who will never see them.
suggested_refs: Suger's account of the relics at the rebuilt choir of Saint-Denis

segments.name: The Company Assembles in the German Dioceses

stops.name: Regensburg, the fresco in the Dominican church
stops.date_confidence: attested as about 1320 by de.wikipedia; no closer dating reached
stops.campa: In the Dominican church of Saint Blasius at Regensburg someone paints a wall with ten saints standing around Christopher. It is the oldest surviving picture of the helpers as a set, and the set is not yet fourteen. The arithmetic is still open: which saints, how many, in what order, and whether the order matters. Already fixed is the manner of the asking. These particular dead are approached together, as one body, and the request made of them is made once and to all of them at the same time.
suggested_refs: The fragmentary Nothelfer fresco in the Dominikanerkirche St. Blasius, Regensburg, oldest known group image

stops.name: Regensburg, the fourteen gathered against the plague
stops.date_confidence: traditional; en.wikipedia gives the fourteenth century and the Black Death without a year, and places the origin in the Rhineland, which de.wikipedia contradicts
stops.campa: The plague comes up the trade roads and the dioceses of Regensburg, Bamberg and Wurzburg begin invoking a fixed company against it: fourteen saints asked at once, in one breath, for one thing. Barbara, Margaret and Catherine stand at the centre of it as the virgin martyrs, each already carrying her own separate cult and feast day before this company ever gathers them in. The disease kills in three days and gives no time to fetch a priest. The helpers are chosen for exactly that, for death arriving faster than the sacraments.
stops.quote: It appears from the invocation of these saints, so widespread in olden times during the plague and other epidemics, that their being grouped as the Fourteen Holy Helpers originated in a like visitation.
stops.quote_source: Bonaventure Hammer, Mary, Help of Christians, and the Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part III, Chapter I
suggested_refs: The plague-era diocesan invocation of the Nothelfer at Regensburg, pin inherited from saint_barbara.journey.json
sources: Hammer, Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part III

stops.name: Regensburg Cathedral, Oswald and Leonhard on the glass
stops.date_confidence: attested for the windows; de.wikipedia says only that they point to the early veneration of the Nothelfer
stops.campa: Windows set into the cathedral show Oswald, king of Northumbria, and Leonhard of Noblac, and German scholarship reads them as evidence of the early cult of the helpers in this diocese. Neither man is among the fourteen the next century will settle on. At this date the company is a habit, and habits vary. A diocese asks the saints it happens to keep; the number and the names shift from parish to parish and from decade to decade, and nothing yet forbids a Northumbrian king from standing in the group.
suggested_refs: The 1360 windows of Regensburg Cathedral showing Oswald and Leonhard

stops.name: Bamberg, the diocese takes up the count
stops.date_confidence: inferred; de.wikipedia names Bamberg among the dioceses of the group's late-medieval fixation without a year
stops.campa: Bamberg takes up the count. The diocese Henry the Second founded on seven hills, with its imperial cathedral and its stone rider, is one of the three or four places German scholarship names as the cradle of the fixed company. Across these sees in the second half of the century the devotion standardises. Prayers are copied from house to house, sermons preached from the same exemplars, painters handed the same commission, until a shepherd anywhere in Franconia knows what fourteen means without being told.
suggested_refs: The diocese of Bamberg as one of the four sees named for the fixation of the Nothelfer

stops.name: Nuremberg, the order closes at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: attested as about 1400 by de.wikipedia; regional lists still substituting Leonard or Sebastian are a reconstruction
stops.campa: By about the turn of the century the fourteen appear in a closed sequence, the same names in the same order, across Regensburg, Bamberg, Wurzburg and Nuremberg. Acacius, Barbara, Blaise, Catherine, Christopher, Cyriacus, Denis, Erasmus, Eustace, George, Giles, Margaret, Pantaleon, Vitus. Regional lists still swap in Leonard or Sebastian here and there, but the shape has hardened. Giles is the only one of them who is not a martyr, admitted on the strength of a wound he refused to have healed.
stops.quote: Sts. Christopher, Barbara, and Catherine were appealed to for protection against a sudden and unprovided death; the aid of St. Giles was implored for making a good confession.
stops.quote_source: Bonaventure Hammer, Mary, Help of Christians, and the Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part III, Chapter I
suggested_refs: The closed late-medieval sequence of the fourteen as given in de.wikipedia, 'Vierzehn Nothelfer'
sources: Hammer, Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part III

stops.name: Domremy, the Ladies' Tree
stops.date_confidence: inherited from catherine_alexandria.journey.json and saint_barbara.journey.json; the Barbara interpolation rests on a 2023 reading of an embroidery and is a reconstruction
stops.campa: On the Meuse a girl of sixteen goes out to the beech the village calls the Ladies' Tree and hears Michael, Catherine and Margaret. Two of the three are of the company. A reading of a 2023 embroidery adds Barbara under the branches, which would put three helpers in a Lorraine meadow speaking to Joan of Arc seventeen years before the Franconian meadow. Nobody in Domremy is counting to fourteen. The saints who arrive are the ones the century has taught the country to expect.
suggested_refs: The Arbre des Dames at Domremy and the 2023 embroidery reading that interpolates Barbara

stops.name: Kloster Langheim, the abbey that owns the field
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the abbey's ownership of the field is attested, the month is set to precede the first apparition
stops.campa: The Cistercians of Langheim hold land on the slope above the Main, and among their tenants is a shepherd named Hermann Leicht, who grazes the abbey's sheep on a field with nothing on it. The house is prosperous, four centuries old, and about to acquire the most lucrative asset in Franconia without spending anything for it. It does not know this yet. For now the field is worth what grass is worth, and the abbey's books carry it as pasture and nothing else.
suggested_refs: Kloster Langheim near Lichtenfels, Cistercian owner of the apparition field

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the shepherd hears a child
stops.date_confidence: contested: en.wikipedia gives 24 September 1445 and the spelling Hermann Leicht, Hammer 1908 gives 22 September and Herman with one m; the discrepancy is not resolved
stops.campa: Bringing the flock in at evening, the shepherd hears crying and sees a child sitting in the field. He goes to lift it and there is nothing there. He says nothing to anyone, because a man alone in a field at dusk who hears a child knows what will be said of him. The field belongs to the abbey, the shepherd is nobody, and the first of the apparitions is witnessed by one person with no standing whatever. Every stone laid on this ground afterwards rests on that evening.
stops.quote: On the evening of September 22, 1445, a young shepherd, Herman Leicht, who was gathering his flock for the homeward drive, heard what seemed to him to be the cry of a child, and looking about, saw a child sitting in a field near by.
stops.quote_source: Bonaventure Hammer, Mary, Help of Christians, and the Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part III, Chapter I
suggested_refs: The apparition field above Kloster Langheim; pin inherited from san_vito, saint_barbara and san_cristobal
sources: Hammer, Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part III

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, fourteen children in red and white
stops.date_confidence: contested: de.wikipedia gives 28 June 1446, while saint_barbara.journey.json and san_vito.journey.json carry 1446-06-24 and giles.journey.json carries 1446-07-28; the three atlas files are unreconciled
stops.campa: The child comes back a second time in the course of the year, and a third time on the day German sources put at the twenty-eighth of June. Now there are fourteen, thirteen more standing around the first, half in red and half in white, with a red cross between them and two candles burning in the air. They tell the shepherd who they are and what they want. It is the one occasion in the whole history of the company when the fourteen speak in their own voice, and what they ask for is a building.
stops.quote: We are the Fourteen Helpers, and desire that a chapel be built for us. Be thou our servant, and we shall serve thee.
stops.quote_source: Bonaventure Hammer, Mary, Help of Christians, and the Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part III, Chapter I, on the apparition of 28 June 1446
suggested_refs: The founding utterance of the group cult, as transmitted by the devotional literature
sources: Hammer, Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part III

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the maidservant rises
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the eighteen-day interval and the cure come from the shrine's own tradition and are not independently attested
stops.campa: Eighteen days after the last apparition a maidservant of Langheim, given up for dead, prays at the field and gets up well. The tradition gives no name for her and no independent witness. What it does give is the mechanism: a vision is one shepherd's word against the world, and a cure is a thing the neighbours can watch walking around the village. From this point the pilgrims come without being summoned, and the abbey that owns the pasture begins to think about an altar.
suggested_refs: The healing of the Langheim maidservant, the miracle credited with beginning the pilgrimage

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the altar consecrated
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; no month or day reached
stops.campa: Three years after the first crying in the field an altar is consecrated on the spot the children named, and the chapel of the Fourteen Helpers exists in law, a devotion with a fixed address for the first time. The place takes the number for its name and keeps it: Vierzehnheiligen, fourteen saints. Vito, Christopher, Barbara and Giles each arrive at this same ground by a separate road out of a separate cult, and each finds the others already waiting there.
suggested_refs: The first chapel of the Fourteen Helpers and its 1448 altar consecration

stops.name: Rome, Nicholas V attaches indulgences
stops.date_confidence: unattested year; en.wikipedia gives no date, only the pontificate of Nicholas V, 1447 to 1455, and the indulgences no longer apply
stops.campa: The pope attaches indulgences to devotion of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, and a Franconian habit becomes something the whole Church can transact in. No year survives for the grant. The pontificate runs from 1447 to 1455 and the source says only that it happened while the joint cult was spreading. The indulgences no longer apply. What they do at the time is turn a shepherd's field into a destination with a price attached, and license every other diocese in Europe to copy the arrangement.
suggested_refs: The indulgences of Nicholas V for devotion to the Fourteen Holy Helpers, year unrecorded

stops.name: Heilsbronn, the altar of the assembled fourteen
stops.date_confidence: attested for the altar; the spread to Sweden, Hungary and Italy is undated in the source
stops.campa: An altar at Heilsbronn Minster shows the fourteen assembled, and by the close of the Middle Ages some eight hundred churches in the German-speaking lands carry their patronage. The devotion has travelled to Sweden, to Hungary, to Italy, on no date any source will give. The count is now an export. A painter takes the commission by name alone, the attributes and the order already understood between him and the parish paying for it, and no diocesan habit needing explanation to either.
suggested_refs: The 1498 Nothelfer altar at Heilsbronn Minster

stops.name: Bindlach, the winged altar and the disputed hand
stops.date_confidence: attested for the altar and the year; the attribution is contested and the painter is not settled
stops.campa: A winged altar is painted for Saint Bartholomew's at Bindlach, its outer panels showing Christ as the Man of Sorrows with the fourteen ranked behind him. In 1687 fire takes the parish church at Lindenhardt and the altar is moved there, which is the name it carries now. The ascription to Matthias Grunewald dates only from 1915, and recent work proposes Hans von Kulmbach instead. The picture is certain, the painter is not, and the place it was made for is not the place it hangs.
suggested_refs: The Lindenhardt altar of 1503, painted for Bindlach, attribution to Grunewald contested since 1915

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the chapel burned in the Peasants' War
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year
stops.campa: The peasants rise across Franconia and Thuringia and burn the chapel in the field. A shrine built for people who die badly is destroyed by people dying badly, and the abbey that has profited from the pilgrimage stands on the wrong side of the rising. A church is put up on the site again afterwards. The number stays. The building can be burned and the pilgrims come back to the same grass, which says plainly enough that what they come for was never in the building.
suggested_refs: The destruction of the first Vierzehnheiligen chapel in the German Peasants' War

stops.name: Ingolstadt, the Wednesday after his feast
stops.date_confidence: attested; the council minute dates the expulsion by the feast of Saint Vitus rather than by the calendar day
stops.campa: The council of Ingolstadt expels a soothsayer and orders the record to say when: the Wednesday after the feast of Saint Vitus. Johann Faust is dated out of a city by a helper's day. In the ordinary German year the fourteen have become the grid the calendar is written on, devotion or no devotion. A clerk reaching for a date reaches for a martyr, and the martyr he reaches for is one of the fourteen, whose feast every man in the room can place without asking.
suggested_refs: The Ingolstadt council minute of 1528 dating Faust's expulsion by the feast of Saint Vitus

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, destroyed a second time
stops.date_confidence: year unattested: de.wikipedia says only that the rebuilt church was destroyed in the Thirty Years' War, 1618 to 1648, and afterwards restored; 1632 is used here for ordering only
stops.campa: The rebuilt church is destroyed again in the Thirty Years' War and again restored. The German source gives no year for it. The war runs from 1618 to 1648 and Franconia is crossed and recrossed by every army in it. Two ruins in a century on the same field, for the same reason: the shrine stands in open country on a good road, which is what made it a pilgrimage site and what makes it a target. The Cistercians rebuild a second time and keep the pilgrimage running.
suggested_refs: The second destruction of the Vierzehnheiligen church during the Thirty Years' War, year unrecorded

stops.name: Langheim, the abbot asks for a new church
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year
stops.campa: Abbot Stephan Mosinger of Langheim obtains permission to pull down the ageing pilgrimage church and put up something worthy of the traffic. The abbey has been living off the shepherd's field for nearly three centuries. It commissions a building organised around the moment the fourteen appeared, with the spot itself, the exact patch of grass, fixed as the point every wall and vault and window must answer to. That one constraint will nearly wreck the design.
suggested_refs: Abbot Stephan Mosinger's petition of 1735 for a new pilgrimage church

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the cornerstone
stops.date_confidence: attested for month and year; no day reached
stops.campa: The foundation stone goes down in April to the design of Balthasar Neumann, the bell-founder's apprentice from Bohemia who became architect of the Wurzburg Residenz and the finest vaulter in Europe. He is fifty-five. The commission is a pilgrimage church for a company of plague saints on a hillside facing the abbey of Banz across the Main valley, and he intends a longitudinal building with the Altar of Grace, the marker of the apparition, standing in the choir where an altar belongs.
suggested_refs: Balthasar Neumann's first design for Vierzehnheiligen, cornerstone laid April 1743

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the altar that cannot be moved
stops.date_confidence: inferred; en.wikipedia describes the sequence without giving a year for the discovery of the changes
stops.campa: Langheim demands cost reductions and a substitute overseer builds the foundations and the three apses to a shortened plan before anyone notices what has happened. The Altar of Grace now falls in the middle of the nave, and it cannot be shifted, because the whole point of it is that it stands where the children stood. Neumann redesigns the interior around the obstacle: three interlocking ovals, the largest of them centred on the altar. The error in the foundations, and not the first design, produces the interior the church is known for.
suggested_refs: The Gnadenaltar at the centre of Neumann's largest oval, dictated by the apparition site

stops.name: Wurzburg, the architect dies
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Neumann dies at Wurzburg on the nineteenth of August, ten years into the work and nineteen years before it is finished. He has seen the ovals set out and the walls rise. He does not see the vault closed, or the plaster laid, or the stuccoists at work in the light he calculated for. Johann Thomas Nissler completes the vaulting. The building is finished by other men to a drawing that solved a problem its author never wanted to be given, and it is called his masterpiece.
suggested_refs: Neumann's death at Wurzburg, 19 August 1753, and the completion of the vault by Johann Thomas Nissler

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the consecration
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Adam Friedrich von Seinsheim, prince-bishop of Wurzburg and of Bamberg at once, consecrates the finished church on the fourteenth of September. Three hundred and twenty-seven years after a shepherd heard crying in a field, the fourteen stand in gilded stucco around the Altar of Grace in the centre of the room, on the exact spot. Everything in the building curves toward that spot. The plan follows a place where a shepherd said he saw a child, and nobody in three centuries was willing to move the mark.
suggested_refs: The consecration of 14 September 1772 by Adam Friedrich von Seinsheim

segments.name: The Altar, the Fire, the Friars

stops.name: Obernburg am Main, the three maidens named by what they carry
stops.date_confidence: inherited byte-identical from saint_barbara, catherine_alexandria and san_vito; the rhyme itself is untraced to any printed original
stops.campa: In the Anna-Kapelle at Obernburg on the Main, Peter Vambach of Erlenbach carves the fourteen in ranked rows, and the rhyme that goes with them names the three maidens by what they hold, a mnemonic built for a congregation that cannot read Latin and needs the saints told apart at a glance. Margaret with the worm, Barbara with the tower, Catherine with the wheel. Barbara, Catherine and Vito each carry their own separate cult, and each is carved on this same altar, pinned to it identically alongside the other eleven.
stops.quote: Margaretha mit dem Wurm, Barbara mit dem Turm, Katharina mit dem Radl, das sind die drei heiligen Madl.
stops.quote_source: German folk mnemonic for the three virgin-martyr Holy Helpers, widely reported in secondary literature; no original chronicle or manuscript source traced
suggested_refs: The Nothelferaltar of Peter Vambach in the Anna-Kapelle, Obernburg am Main

stops.name: Langheim, the abbey dissolved
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year
stops.campa: Bavarian secularisation dissolves the Cistercian house of Langheim, disperses the monks and takes the lands. The abbey that owned the field, authenticated the visions, collected the pilgrimage and paid for Neumann is abolished by an administrative act, three hundred and fifty-eight years after a shepherd on its payroll saw something in the grass. The basilica stands. The institution that built it does not. The pilgrims, who were never the abbey's in the first place, keep arriving.
suggested_refs: The 1803 dissolution of Kloster Langheim under Bavarian secularisation

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, lightning takes the towers
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; no month or day reached
stops.campa: Lightning strikes the basilica and takes the organ, the roof structure and both towers. It is the third destruction on this ground in three centuries, the first two by human armies. Ludwig the First of Bavaria, who has no abbey left to call on, sends Franciscans in 1839 to take charge of the church and see it restored, and the friars are there still. A shrine to saints invoked against sudden death by fire and storm is unroofed by a bolt out of the sky in the reign of a king who collects buildings.
suggested_refs: The lightning strike of 1835 and the Franciscan custody granted by Ludwig I in 1839

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, raised to minor basilica
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; de.wikipedia and en.wikipedia agree
stops.campa: Leo the Thirteenth raises the church to the rank of minor basilica, the second in Germany to be given the title. The cult it was built for has by then been quietly demoted in the wider Church, its members' feasts kept in Franconia and forgotten elsewhere, and the building has outgrown the devotion. What Rome honours in 1897 is Neumann's ovals as much as the fourteen, and a pilgrimage that has not stopped since a maidservant of Langheim got up off her bed and walked.
suggested_refs: The 1897 elevation of Vierzehnheiligen to basilica minor by Leo XIII

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the barrio on the third hill
stops.date_confidence: inherited from san_cristobal.journey.json; the barrio pin is nominal and carries no relic or legend
stops.campa: Across the ocean a Buenos Aires barrio carries the name San Cristobal, taken from the saint with no relic behind it and no legend attached to the ground. Christopher, one of the fourteen, arrives in the southern hemisphere as a street plan. Emin Arslan, consul of the Ottomans in the same city, shares the pin. A company assembled in Bavaria against the plague ends up, by way of empire and language, as the name of a neighbourhood where nobody counts to fourteen and nobody needs to.
suggested_refs: The barrio of San Cristobal, Buenos Aires, shared pin with emin_arslan.journey.json

stops.name: Rome, four names come off the calendar
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the revision
stops.campa: The revised General Roman Calendar drops the individual feasts of Barbara, Catherine of Alexandria, Christopher and Margaret of Antioch from the universal observance of the Church. None of the four is decanonised and all keep their days on local calendars, where Franconia goes on keeping them. Ten of the fourteen are untouched. The reform is aimed at the historicity of the lives, and the four removed are precisely the four whose lives the scholars could not stand behind.
suggested_refs: The 1969 revision of the General Roman Calendar and the four Helpers removed from universal observance

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the Rieger organ
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year
stops.campa: A new organ by Rieger, sixty-eight registers, goes into the basilica a hundred and sixty-four years after lightning destroyed the instrument that stood there. It is voiced for a room whose acoustics were settled by a shepherd's inability to move a patch of grass. The three ovals Neumann was forced into carry sound in a way a nave would not. The building keeps working as a building long after the argument about which fourteen saints belong inside it has gone quiet.
suggested_refs: The 1999 Rieger organ of 68 registers at Vierzehnheiligen

stops.name: Vatican City, Catherine restored
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year
stops.campa: John Paul the Second restores Catherine of Alexandria to the universal calendar as an optional memorial on the twenty-fifth of November, decades after a reform of the calendar had struck her from it for want of reliable evidence that she had ever lived. One of the four comes back and the other three do not. Catherine, with her wheel, is the only member of the company whose standing in Rome has moved twice inside one lifetime. The count of fourteen was never affected by any of it. Nothing in Franconia was waiting for permission.
suggested_refs: The 2004 restoration of the optional memorial of Catherine of Alexandria on 25 November

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the season from May to October
stops.date_confidence: present practice; the year is nominal
stops.campa: The pilgrimages run from May to October, as they have since there was a road up the hill. The basilica and the former abbey of Banz face each other across the Main valley, and the locals call the pair the Goldene Pforte, the golden gate into Franconia. Six hundred years after the plague that made the count necessary, the fourteen are asked for the same things they were assembled for: the throat, the belly, the cattle, the storm, and a death with warning enough to prepare for.
suggested_refs: The seasonal pilgrimage calendar at Vierzehnheiligen and the Goldene Pforte with Schloss Banz
